title: Reversible emergency metabolic suspension

concept.text: Reversible emergency metabolic suspension would rapidly lower a critically injured patient’s whole-body metabolic activity, preserve the brain and other organs during a delay to definitive treatment, and then permit safe restoration of circulation, temperature and function. Emergency preservation and resuscitation (EPR) provides a research foundation through profound cooling that reduces oxygen consumption and helps preserve cellular viability. The proposed innovation combines reliable induction, sustained preservation and recovery into an emergency treatment that could be delivered across realistic care settings.

The documented clinical motivation centers on cardiac arrest caused by catastrophic blood loss. In that setting, preservation could create time for surgeons to repair injuries before circulation is restored. The broader proposed capability includes varied emergency patients and treatment beginning without a fully equipped operating room at the point of injury. Patient selection, duration and delivery methods for that broader scope remain unresolved.

significance.text: If sufficiently rapid, safe and reversible suppression could be achieved, it could substantially extend the interval available for transport and surgical repair. Lower oxygen demand could delay ischemic injury while definitive care is unavailable, preserving the possibility of meaningful neurological recovery. Several hours of usable preservation would be transformative for patients whose injuries otherwise become fatal before treatment can begin. That duration remains a proposed goal for the complete capability.

Remote-care benefits would depend on portable equipment, consumables, trained responders, suitable transport and access to definitive treatment. A preservation interval would have clinical value only if the patient could subsequently receive hemorrhage control, resuscitation and recovery care. The review’s deployment discussion therefore makes practical delivery part of the breakthrough itself.

Conditional synthesis. Disaster response could benefit if preservation systems were deployable at sufficient scale and receiving hospitals could treat patients within the additional time gained. Metabolic suspension would temporarily reduce the urgency imposed by oxygen deprivation while leaving the underlying injuries to be treated. Its impact would consequently depend on both biological preservation and the capacity of the surrounding emergency-care system.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is dependable induction and reversal of profound whole-body metabolic suppression in emergency patients, with preserved brain and organ function. A successful system must lower metabolic demand quickly enough to protect tissue during severe circulatory failure, sustain that protection during treatment delays and restore physiological function safely. Extension from the narrow exsanguinating-trauma setting to varied emergency conditions would require evidence for each additional patient population.

Bleeding and clot formation create a difficult treatment balance. Patients may have continuing hemorrhage, while the preservation and extracorporeal-resuscitation process must also contend with clotting. Cooling and reduced oxygen consumption must provide adequate protection despite existing oxygen deprivation. Subsequent reperfusion and rewarming introduce further risks, so restoration of circulation and temperature must be integrated with injury repair and protection of vulnerable organs.

Delivery remains an engineering and operational barrier. The clinical protocol described in the review involves thoracotomy, aortic cannulation, cold infusion, cardiopulmonary bypass and controlled rewarming, supported by highly trained personnel. Achieving the proposed point-of-injury capability would require a practical way to initiate preservation under emergency conditions and maintain continuity through transport, definitive treatment and recovery. Portable systems and simplified deployment remain development needs.

current_state.text: The review by Remondelli and colleagues, published on 10 April 2026, describes preservation of learning and memory after up to 60 minutes of hypothermic arrest in swine. It separately reports more than 75% survival at six weeks with intact neurological function in a complex abdominal and vascular injury pig model using the optimized parameters. The duration is explicitly attached to the learning-and-memory study in the supplied review. The complex-injury result is described as using those parameters, which leaves the precise duration-to-outcome linkage dependent on the underlying primary study. Both findings are secondary reports of controlled animal experiments.

Reference 35 in the review identifies a 2008 dog study whose title reports neurological recovery after three hours of profoundly hypothermic cardiac arrest following rapid exsanguination. The supplied evidence establishes that the review cites this result. The primary study’s methods, controls, outcome assessments and reproducibility were outside the supplied inspection, limiting conclusions about how broadly that duration applies.

For human translation, the review reports that the EPR-CAT feasibility trial was terminated because of enrollment difficulties. It describes an invasive specialist protocol and planned assessment of survival to hospital discharge without significant neurological sequelae, alongside longer-term neurological outcomes, organ failure and complications. Human efficacy remains unestablished in the supplied evidence. The termination report comes from the review, with independent registry confirmation still outstanding.

The supplied review relied on an identity-verified, complete article XML containing the narrative and references. The research record reports access through an indexed version and a 403 response to a direct PDF fetch. PDF page numbers and figure imagery were outside the supplied validation, so the relevant locators are the sections “DHCA under planned conditions” and “Clinical investigations of EPR,” together with references 35–37. The animal findings remain dated reports with these access boundaries. Coverage of subsequent developments through 1 November 2026 is unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Independently replicated, controlled large-animal studies should show survival with preserved learning, memory and organ function after several hours of induced suspension, incorporating realistic injury patterns and delays to definitive treatment. Protocols should define when preservation begins, how duration is measured, how circulation and temperature are restored, and how functional recovery is assessed over time. Several hours is a proposed test target whose clinical relevance would depend on the intended use.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated large-animal studies show functional survival after several hours’ suspension

completion_criteria.text: Proposed human demonstration. Comparative trials should show improved long-term neurologically favorable survival against the best feasible emergency care in explicitly defined eligible populations. Evaluation should include organ failure, complications and the reliability of induction and reversal. The review’s EPR-CAT endpoints provide a clinical foundation for assessing meaningful survival and recovery, while the comparative and replication requirements here are proposed criteria.
completion_criteria.label: Improved long-term neurologically favorable survival versus best feasible emergency care

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration. A system intended for point-of-injury or remote use should demonstrate that trained teams can initiate preservation, maintain it during realistic transport delays and transfer patients into definitive treatment with reproducible outcomes outside specialist centers. Testing should establish equipment, consumable, staffing and care-capacity requirements, along with the injury types, patient groups and delay intervals within which benefit is demonstrated. Finite studies would establish a tested range of use, with broader applicability requiring further evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible preservation outside specialist centers through transfer into definitive treatment

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. EMR-02, “Neurologically intact recovery after prolonged untreated cardiac arrest,” shares the goal of preserving or recovering brain function after interrupted circulation. EMR-01 focuses on deliberately inducing a protective state early enough to extend the treatment window. EMR-02 addresses recovery after a prolonged untreated interval, when substantial injury may already have accumulated. EMR-11, “Acute rescue and repair of injured vital tissue,” could contribute treatments for residual organ damage during recovery from suspension.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-03, “Field treatment that safely stops inaccessible internal bleeding,” and EMR-04, “Inexpensive, universally compatible emergency blood replacement,” address major causes and consequences of traumatic circulatory collapse. They could complement metabolic preservation by controlling hemorrhage and restoring circulatory support. EMR-01 adds a proposed means of reducing tissue oxygen demand during the interval required to deliver those treatments.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-05, “A portable, broad-spectrum emergency diagnostic system,” could support patient selection and identify injuries requiring definitive treatment. EMR-08, “Non-surgical rescue oxygenation for otherwise unmanageable airways,” concerns maintaining oxygen delivery when airway management fails. Metabolic suspension addresses oxygen demand and preservation during compromised circulation. The interaction between these capabilities would require testing within specific emergency pathways.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-06, “Rapid reversal of septic shock and its harmful host response,” and EMR-07, “Broad-spectrum emergency antidote platform,” target causes of physiological collapse that might motivate future investigation of preservation as a bridge to treatment. Their inclusion in the roster supplies possible relationships, while evidence for metabolic suspension in sepsis or poisoning remains outside the supplied record.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-09, “Effective early prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder after emergency care,” and EMR-10, “Rapid, potent non-opioid treatment for severe acute pain,” address additional dimensions of emergency treatment and recovery. They could accompany a future suspension pathway through pain management and longer-term psychological care. Evidence for these interactions remains outside the supplied record.

Existing surgical hypothermia, extracorporeal circulation and reperfusion research provide technical context for EMR-01. Accidental hypothermia survival and cellular recovery platforms also inform questions about tissue preservation and recovery. Their distinct circumstances and endpoints limit extrapolation to deliberately induced, deployable whole-body emergency suspension with durable neurological recovery.

unresolved_issues: The exact duration and protocol-to-outcome linkage in the complex-injury pig model require verification in the primary study.
Primary methods, controls, neurological assessments and reproducibility of the 2008 three-hour dog result remain unverified.
The supplied record lacks independent trial-registry confirmation and human efficacy results for EPR-CAT.
Later developments through 1 November 2026 remain unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.
Eligible patient groups, acceptable adverse-event rates, preservation duration definitions and thresholds for preserved cognitive and organ function require prospective specification.
The feasibility and benefit of initiation outside specialist centers, including remote and disaster deployment, remain undemonstrated in the supplied evidence.
Applicability beyond exsanguinating traumatic arrest remains a proposed extension requiring population-specific evidence.

brief.title: A reversible body slowdown for emergency care
possible: Someone bleeding catastrophically could gain time to reach surgery. Rapidly slowing the body’s activity would reduce its need for oxygen, protecting the brain and other organs until injuries could be repaired. Care teams could then restore blood flow, warmth and function.
why: Patients whose injuries would otherwise become fatal before treatment could have a chance to survive with their thinking and memory intact. Extra time could help emergency teams transport patients and give surgeons a longer window to stop the bleeding.

sources.showed: Their review describes animal experiments using profound cooling to preserve function during stopped circulation. It also reports that a human feasibility trial ended because too few patients could be enrolled.
sources.quote: In extreme cases, patients can survive extended periods of circulatory arrest, as case reports of successful resuscitation without long-term sequelae have been observed.
sources.cited_for: Cooling provides a research foundation for protecting patients while circulation is stopped.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish that deliberately induced emergency preservation improves human survival and recovery.

sources.showed: In a small pig study, mild cooling reduced oxygen use after severe blood loss. Clotting changes reversed with warming, but survival did not improve significantly.
sources.quote: Rewarming reversed the coagulation changes induced by hypothermia.
sources.cited_for: Controlled cooling can reduce oxygen demand after traumatic blood loss, while also changing clotting.
sources.not_established: Mild cooling during blood-loss shock does not demonstrate prolonged whole-body suspension or lasting recovery of brain function.

shown: The review reports that pigs retained learning and memory after up to 60 minutes with circulation stopped under deep cooling. Separate experiments involving complex injuries achieved survival with intact brain function. These are controlled animal results.
missing: Emergency patients still need a reliable way to enter and recover from profound body slowdown with brain and organ function preserved.
Protection must work despite ongoing bleeding and safely manage clotting, restored blood flow and rewarming.
A practical system must begin preservation outside specialist centers and sustain it through transport, surgery and recovery.

milestones.label: Replicated animal survival after several hours with function preserved
milestones.explanation: Independent large-animal studies would have to show survival with preserved learning, memory and organ function after several hours of suspension under realistic injuries and delays. This would establish durable protection.

milestones.label: Better long-term survival with brain function preserved
milestones.explanation: Human trials would have to show better long-term survival with brain function preserved than the best feasible emergency care. This would establish a benefit for clearly defined patient groups.

milestones.label: Reliable preservation outside specialist centers through transfer to treatment
milestones.explanation: Trained teams would have to reproduce successful preservation outside specialist centers through realistic transport delays and transfer into definitive treatment. This would establish practical delivery.

uncertain: Which injuries and patient groups could benefit beyond cardiac arrest caused by catastrophic blood loss?
How should preservation time, acceptable complications and lasting recovery of thinking and organ function be defined?
How consistently can prolonged animal preservation results be reproduced under realistic emergency conditions?

page.title: Emergency preservation and resuscitation for traumatic arrest
page.definition: Emergency preservation and resuscitation (EPR) would cool a patient who remains pulseless after massive blood loss from a penetrating injury. Surgeons use cooling before planned circulatory arrest in some heart and aortic operations. In EPR, ice-cold saline would be infused into the aorta after arrest to reduce the organs’ oxygen demand while surgeons stop the bleeding. A heart-lung machine would then restore blood flow and rewarm the patient, with the aim of survival without major disability.

goal.need: Across 4,620 emergency chest operations for blunt or penetrating trauma, 7.4% of patients survived. Even with fluid replacement and direct heart massage, the brain can suffer irreversible damage within minutes if bleeding prevents blood flow from returning. For a patient still pulseless after a penetrating injury, cooling could give surgeons time to repair the injury while preserving the chance of recovery without major disability. That requires a source of bleeding surgeons can control and a team ready to restore circulation on bypass.

completion.title: An EPR-treated trauma patient leaves hospital with a Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended score above 5.
completion.criterion: An eligible EPR-CAT patient undergoes cooling, surgical bleeding control and delayed resuscitation with cardiopulmonary bypass, then leaves hospital with a Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended score of 6, 7 or 8. A score of 6 denotes upper moderate disability. Scores of 7 and 8 denote lower and upper good recovery.
completion.set_by: EPR-CAT investigators, adopting the discharge endpoint suggested by the US Food and Drug Administration for the feasibility study.
completion.threshold_quote: survival to hospital discharge without major disability (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended >5)
completion.basis: One qualifying discharge would establish human proof of concept. The trial’s objective was to compare this outcome with concurrent or historical controls. A single recovery cannot establish comparative efficacy. EPR-CAT was terminated, and the registry update posted on 16 June 2026 contains no outcome values.

milestones.title: Swine retain learning and memory after 60 minutes at 10°C during vascular repair.
milestones.criterion: Swine undergo vascular repair during 60 minutes of low-flow cardiopulmonary bypass at a core temperature of 10°C and are followed for six weeks. After repair, previously untrained animals learn to retrieve food from color-coded boxes with performance comparable to controls, and animals trained before injury retain the task.
milestones.set_by: Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences investigators, in Alam and colleagues’ published 2002 swine experimental protocol; a study-specific benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: Cooling continued until core temperature reached 10 degrees C, and this was maintained for 60 minutes using low-flow cardiopulmonary bypass.

milestones.title: Swine survive six weeks after vascular, colon and splenic repair during 60 minutes of low-flow EPR.
milestones.criterion: Swine survive for six weeks after combined vascular, colon and splenic injuries are repaired during 60 minutes of low-flow cardiopulmonary bypass at 10°C, followed by rewarming at 0.5°C/min. Follow-up shows intact neurological function, normal capacity to learn new skills and no long-term organ dysfunction.
milestones.set_by: Massachusetts General Hospital and collaborating investigators, in Sailhamer and colleagues’ published 2007 swine experimental protocol; a study-specific benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: All surviving animals were neurologically intact, displayed normal learning capacity, and had no longterm organ dysfunction.

milestones.title: EPR cools a trauma patient’s estimated brain temperature to 10°C and rectal temperature below 30°C.
milestones.criterion: After ice-cold saline infusion into the aorta, an eligible EPR-CAT patient reaches a tympanic or nasopharyngeal temperature of 10°C, used to estimate brain temperature, and a rectal temperature below 30°C.
milestones.set_by: University of Maryland and University of Pittsburgh investigators, in the final EPR-CAT protocol developed under an FDA Investigational Device Exemption.
milestones.threshold_quote:
Cooling will continue until Tty or Tnp is 10°C,
and rectal temperature is less than 30°C.

milestones.title: After EPR and bleeding control, a patient regains circulation sufficient to stop cardiopulmonary bypass.
milestones.criterion: After surgical bleeding control, an EPR-treated patient undergoes reperfusion and rewarming, targeting 0.5°C/min until 36°C, and recovers spontaneous circulation sufficiently stable for weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass.
milestones.set_by: University of Maryland and University of Pittsburgh investigators, in the EPR-CAT protocol’s post-repair resuscitation and decannulation steps.
milestones.threshold_quote: sufficiently stable spontaneous circulation to be weaned

milestones.title: Dogs recover normal neurological function after 60 minutes of circulatory arrest at 15°C.
milestones.criterion: After 30 minutes of hemorrhagic shock at a mean arterial pressure of 40 mm Hg, dogs are cooled to 15°C on bypass, undergo 60 minutes of circulatory arrest, and are reperfused and rewarmed on bypass. They survive beyond 72 hours and attain a best neurological deficit score of 0%, the study’s normal score.
milestones.set_by: University of Pittsburgh investigators, in the 60-minute arm of Tisherman and colleagues’ 1990 canine protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: Best neurologic deficit scores (ND) (0% = normal, 100% = brain death) were 0 +/- 0% (normal) in Group 1

milestones.title: Surgeons control bleeding and restart bypass with total circulatory arrest under one hour.
milestones.criterion: After the patient reaches the cooling targets, surgeons secure hemostasis during circulatory arrest. They then restart cardiopulmonary bypass for reperfusion and rewarming, meeting the protocol’s goal of less than one hour of total circulatory arrest.
milestones.set_by: EPR-CAT investigators, in the master protocol and the published final protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: The goal will be to keep the total time of circulatory arrest under 1 hour

not_found: No published EPR-CAT patient-level cooling measurements, successful bypass-weaning outcomes or discharge disability scores were found.
The original ClinicalTrials.gov study text and API could not be retrieved; the 2026 registry update was accessible through a mirror.
No definitive clinical efficacy success rule beyond the EPR-CAT patient-level endpoint was found.

results.finding: In 9 swine undergoing vascular repair during 60 minutes of low-flow bypass, survivors learned the food retrieval task comparably to controls or retained prior training.
results.detail: Seven of nine swine survived. The abstract gives the enrollment counts by training status but does not specify how the seven survivors were distributed across those groups.
results.quote: their capacity to learn new skills was no different than for control animals. All pretrained animals demonstrated complete memory retention.

results.finding: All 22 surviving swine displayed normal learning capacity.
results.detail: The survivor count is derived from the reported group sizes and six-week survival rates.
results.quote: All surviving animals were neurologically intact, displayed normal learning capacity, and had no longterm organ dysfunction.

results.finding: Six-week survival was 75% among 8 swine with combined vascular, colon and splenic injuries.
results.quote: Six-week survival rates were 90% in group 1, 87.5% in group 2, and 75% in group 3 (p > 0.05).

results.finding: In six EPR-treated pigs, mean brain temperature reached 16.7°C after a cold saline aortic flush.
results.detail: The abstract gives no tympanic, nasopharyngeal or rectal temperatures.
results.quote: In the EPR group, brain temperature decreased from 38.5 degrees C +/- 0.2 degrees C to 16.7 degrees C +/- 2.5 degrees C within 235 +/- 27 secs.

results.finding: Five of six EPR-treated pigs regained spontaneous circulation.
results.quote: Five animals achieved restoration of spontaneous circulation and survived to 9 days: two pigs with overall performance category 2 and three pigs with overall performance category 3.

results.finding: Of 10 swine treated for vascular injuries alone, nine survived to six weeks and showed normal learning capacity.
results.quote: All surviving animals were neurologically intact, displayed normal learning capacity, and had no longterm organ dysfunction.

results.finding: Among eight swine treated for combined vascular, colon and splenic injuries, six survived to six weeks with intact neurological function, normal learning and no long-term organ dysfunction.
results.detail: One animal died of acute cardiac failure early after surgery, and one died of bowel obstruction on postoperative day nine.
results.quote: Six-week survival rates were 90% in group 1, 87.5% in group 2, and 75% in group 3 (p > 0.05).

results.finding: In the 15-dog study, the 60-minute arrest group achieved a best neurologic deficit score of 0%.
results.detail: The supplied abstract gives the total sample size but does not specify the size of the 60-minute group.
results.quote: Best neurologic deficit scores (ND) (0% = normal, 100% = brain death) were 0 +/- 0% (normal) in Group 1, 10 +/- 8% (mild disability) in Group 2, and 27 +/- 24% in Group 3.
